Burleigh County by the numbers

What is Burleigh County, North Dakota?

Burleigh County is in south-central North Dakota, and Bismarck is both its county seat and its largest city. The Dakota Territory legislature created it on January 4, 1873, and it was organized on July 16 of that year.

The county covers 1,668 square miles, of which about 36 are water. Its neighbors are Sheridan County to the north, Kidder to the east, Emmons to the south, Morton to the southwest, Oliver to the west and McLean to the northwest. The Missouri River runs south-southeast along the lower western edge, creeks drain the center, and the land is semi-arid with low rolling hills, partly farmed. The highest point is 2,060 feet on the upper east boundary, and the county holds several lakes and parts of national wildlife refuges, including Canfield Lake, Florence Lake and Long Lake.

The 2020 census counted 98,458 residents. Bis-Man Transit (Capital Area Transit) and Jefferson Lines serve the area. The 2024 American Community Survey puts median household income at $88,701, with 42.4 percent of adults holding a bachelor's degree or higher.

Which Burleigh County taxing districts show up on a bill?

Every parcel sits in a taxing district that combines a city or township with a school district, and each combination has its own total mill levy. The county's 2025 mill levy sheet is the clearest way to see this. These are figures from that sheet:

Taxing district2025 total mills
City of Bismarck237.10
City of Lincoln227.55
City of Wing204.52
City of Regan272.08
South Wilton274.74
Menoken (rural district)109.40
Canfield (rural, three listings)194.61, 153.92, 153.92

Rural parcels outside any city usually carry lower totals because they pay no city levy, and several townships have more than one listing because they lie in more than one school or fire district. A mill is one thousandth of a dollar, and the county lists mill levy sheets for 2022 through 2025 on its taxes and levies page.

The county explains that it prepares, collects and distributes the tax, but the County Commission has no authority over the cities, townships, schools and other districts that set levies. Each subdivision submits its budget to the county auditor by October 10, and the levy follows from the funds needed divided by the subdivision's taxable valuation.

Who assesses property in Burleigh County?

The Burleigh County Tax Equalization Office oversees valuation of real property across the county, and Allan Vietmeier is listed as director. The office is at 221 N 5th Street, Bismarck, with mailing address PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506, and phones listed as (701) 222-6693 and (701) 222-6691.

It works under North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-10.1 and uses computer assisted mass appraisal software. It updates records through reappraisal, building permits and sales review. After the State Board of Equalization approves values, the office sends certified values to the auditor to compute tax. The State Tax Commissioner checks the results with a sales ratio analysis to confirm properties are valued at market.

Local assessors do the first valuation. Property outside Bismarck city limits can be looked up at burleigh.northdakotaassessors.com, and city property is on the City of Bismarck's property information page. The county's own annual timeline is:

  • February 1: the local assessor establishes values
  • April: the local board of equalization reviews them
  • June: the county board reviews the local boards' recommendations
  • August: the State Board of Equalization reviews the county boards' work
  • October 10: each taxing subdivision sends its budget to the county auditor

What are the Burleigh County property tax dates and penalties?

Real estate tax is due in two installments: the first on March 1 and the second on October 15. Paying everything, including special assessments, by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount on the consolidated tax. The county mails statements each December, as state law requires by December 26, and mobile home statements go out in January.

DateReal estate, first installment and specialsReal estate, second installment
March 23%n/a
May 16%n/a
July 19%n/a
October 15 or 1612% (Oct. 15)6% (Oct. 16)

Mobile homes follow a separate calendar. The first installment is due February 28 and takes 2 percent penalties starting March 1, rising 2 points on the first of each month through June. The second is due June 30, with penalties from July 1 through October. The county's discount applies to mobile home tax as well when paid by February 15.

The county advises that a payment must arrive, or be postmarked, on or before the deadline to receive the discount. It cannot guarantee USPS or courier delivery, and it guarantees date stamps only for the drop box or hand delivery at the Auditor's Office.

How do you pay a Burleigh County tax bill?

You can pay online, by phone or by mail, and each has a cost. The online portal is the county's property search, which finds a parcel by address (use as few characters as you can) or by the parcel number printed on the statement. Owner names on the portal reflect the most recent tax statement.

  • Online or by phone at 1-800-272-9829 with jurisdiction code 4434; a property number is required for phone payment
  • E-check fee of $3.98 for amounts under $10,000 and $19.92 for $10,000 or more
  • Credit card online or by phone only, with a 3.61 percent fee and a $1.52 minimum
  • Mail to Burleigh County Auditor, PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506

If you did not receive a statement, the county treasurer is the contact at 701-222-6718.

How do you appeal a Burleigh County assessment?

Appeal informally through the boards of equalization or formally through abatement.

The abatement route runs through N.D.C.C. 57-23-04. An application goes to the county auditor on or before November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent, and the board of county commissioners may abate or refund the tax in whole or in part. The Tax Equalization page links the abatement application. It does not state meeting dates or appeal deadlines for the boards, so confirm them with the office.

Outside Bismarck the first stop is the township or city board of equalization, which meets in April, so the first office to contact can differ from the city's.

What happens to delinquent Burleigh County property?

Property is subject to foreclosure of the tax lien when taxes, specials and penalties are unpaid into the third year. The Auditor/Treasurer tracks delinquent parcels, notifies interested parties and holds an annual sale. A delinquent property tax list and the terms of the annual sale are posted on the county site.

StepTiming
Foreclosure notice to owner and occupantsBefore June 1
Notice published in the county newspaperBefore August 1
Tax lien foreclosure date; pay in full by 5 p.m.October 1
Sale notice posted, at least 15 days beforePosted in the office and online
Annual tax saleThird Tuesday of November

An owner can bring the account current between October 2 and the sale by paying all taxes, specials, interest and penalties before the sale begins. The county page does not describe redemption after the sale, so read the sale terms or ask the treasurer.

What credits and exemptions does Burleigh County list?

The Tax Equalization page lists exemptions for permanent wheelchair confinement, blindness and paraplegic disabled veterans with VA adaptive housing, a farm residence exemption, and a separate application for new or expanding businesses. It also lists a homestead credit for people 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, with income under $70,000, and a disabled veteran credit that requires an honorable discharge and a VA rating of 50 percent or more.

The county's deadline shown for the homestead credit was March 31, 2024, which has passed, so check with the office before relying on any date.

How does paying tax at closing work for a Burleigh County sale?

At closing the title company pays current and past taxes from the seller's proceeds. Ask the county auditor for a figure good through the closing date, because the penalty step-ups on March 2, May 1, July 1 and October 15 can change the number. If the house is in a city, ask the city for any remaining special assessment balance, since the city, not the county, takes those payments for city property. For rural property, special assessments are paid at the county Auditor/Treasurer's office.

We buy Burleigh County houses as-is, including ones with back taxes. We cannot promise a price before seeing the property, and you owe nothing if you decline our offer.

More questions about Burleigh County, ND Property Tax Guide

Where is the Burleigh County treasurer's office?

It is at 221 N 5th Street, Bismarck, ND 58501. The main phone is 701-222-6718, and the mailing address is PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506.

How is property tax calculated in Burleigh County?

Assessed value is 50 percent of market value, and taxable value is 9 percent of assessed value for residential property and 10 percent for commercial and agricultural property. The consolidated tax is taxable value times the combined mill levy of the taxing districts.

When is the Burleigh County tax sale?

The annual sale is held on the third Tuesday of November, for property whose tax lien foreclosure date was October 1. You can pay up to the start of the sale.

How can I get the 5 percent discount in Burleigh County?

Pay the entire tax, including special assessments, by February 15. Payments received or postmarked after that date do not get the discount.

Who do I contact to dispute my value?

Call the Burleigh County Tax Equalization Office at (701) 222-6693 or your local city or township assessor. For a formal appeal, apply for abatement with the county auditor by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent.

Where is Morton County, North Dakota?

Morton County is in south-central North Dakota, with the Missouri River running along its east boundary and Mandan as its county seat and largest city. It covers about 1,945 square miles, making it the seventh largest county in the state by area.

The 2020 census counted 33,291 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 34,601. That ranks it sixth in population among the state's counties. Neighbors are Oliver, Burleigh, Emmons, Sioux, Grant, Stark and Mercer counties.

Morton County is part of the Bismarck metropolitan area. Burleigh County and the state capital of Bismarck lie across the river, and the county tax offices sit in Mandan.

What is the landscape like and how did the county form?

The terrain is low rolling hills cut by gullies and drainages, with level farmland in places. The Cannonball River runs along part of the south boundary, and Lake Oahe, Lake Patricia and the Lake Patricia National Wildlife Refuge are among the water features. The high point is 2,375 feet.

The Dakota Territory legislature created the county on January 8, 1873, and it was organized on November 5, 1878. A settlement appeared in 1878 after the Northern Pacific Railroad chose a western approach to its Missouri River bridge, and it later became Mandan. In 1916 land was split off to form Grant County, which fixed the current boundaries.

A 72-mile stretch of the Dakota Access Pipeline passes through the county.

What is Mandan like for homeowners and sellers?

Mandan is on I-94 just west of the Missouri River and across from Bismarck. The city's business development office describes the economy as diverse, naming oil, energy, agriculture, tourism, healthcare, government services, technology and manufacturing.

Interstate 94 and Highways 1806, 6 and 25 carry traffic through the city, and people from towns such as Hebron, New Salem, Flasher and Glen Ullin travel to or through Mandan for routine purchases. The Bismarck airport has daily Delta service to Minneapolis-St. Paul, United to Denver and American to Dallas-Fort Worth and Chicago. BNSF and the Dakota Missouri Valley Western Railroad provide freight rail.

  • I-94 corridor in north Mandan
  • East Mandan along Memorial Highway near the river
  • Main Street and downtown Mandan

These are the areas the city names for retail-ready and commercial development.

Who assesses property in Morton County?

Two offices value property here. The county Tax Equalization Office oversees assessments in unincorporated areas and in cities and townships that contract with the county, while the City of Mandan runs its own Assessing and Building Inspections departments inside city limits.

The county assesses residential and commercial property at market value as of February 1 each year, and farmland follows the state's agricultural valuation guide. The county is split into ten zones so each property is reassessed at least once every ten years. Owners in the current zone receive a letter offering an assessor appointment or a property detail sheet to complete.

Building permits follow the same split. The county Building Inspector handles unincorporated areas, plus Almont and Glen Ullin at those cities' request. Flasher, Hebron and New Salem issue their own.

What credits can lower a Morton County bill?

Morton County lists three programs that reduce residential tax, each tied to the owner's status.

  • Homestead Property Tax Credit: owners 65 or older or disabled whose household income does not exceed $70,000 after medical deductions
  • Disabled Veterans Property Tax Credit: veterans with a disability of 50 percent or more
  • Primary Residence Credit, administered by the State Tax Commissioner

The county also publishes a property tax calculator and a farm residence exemption page through the Tax Equalization Office.

Who is the Morton County Treasurer and when are taxes due?

The Morton County Treasurer's office is at 210 2nd Ave NW, Mandan, ND 58554, phone 701-667-3310, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. except holidays. The treasurer is elected to a four-year term and collects real estate and mobile home taxes.

The office mails statements and delinquent notices and gives lenders the figures they need for escrow accounts. Taxes are due January 1 and payable without penalty through March 1, and paying the full year by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount.

DateEvent
February 1Valuation date
AprilCity or township board of equalization
Early JuneCounty board of equalization
AugustState board of equalization
By December 26Statements mailed
February 155% discount deadline
March 1First installment due
October 15Second installment due

The penalty schedule in North Dakota Century Code section 57-20-01 adds 3 percent after March 1, then 3 percent on May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

How do I appeal a Morton County assessment?

Call the assessor right away and ask for a review, since many questions are settled without a hearing. Assessment letters carry each property's proposed true and full value.

If that does not resolve it, appeal at the local equalization meetings, which cover the current year's valuation. Cities and townships meet in April, the Morton County Board of Equalization meets in early June, and the State Board of Equalization completes its review in August. The state board can lower a value only if you appeared at both the local and county boards.

You can also file an abatement covering the current and previous years. The county's page puts the deadline at November 1 and says the applicant has the burden of proof, so confirm the year with the office. Forms are on the State Tax Commissioner's site or from the county.

What is the Morton County delinquent tax timeline?

A property becomes subject to tax lien foreclosure when taxes, specials and interest stay delinquent in the third year. The county auditor tracks these parcels, notifies interested parties and holds an annual sale.

WhenStep
Before June 1Foreclosure notice goes to the owner, occupants and others with an interest
Before August 1Notice of delinquent property published in the official county newspaper
October 1, 5 p.m.Everything owed must be paid to the County Treasurer
After October 1Owner can still pay in full before the sale starts
Third Tuesday of NovemberAnnual sale

Sale notices are posted at least 15 days before the sale in the auditor's office and on the county website, and published at least 10 days before in the county newspaper.

How does selling a Morton County house with tax due work?

You can sell and pay the tax from the proceeds, and a cash buyer can close faster than a lender-financed sale. The title company gets the payoff from the Treasurer and pays it at closing.

The delinquency calendar is the reason to act early. Once a county takes a tax deed, an owner can buy the property back only before resale, either in full or under an installment contract with at least 25 percent paid in cash, according to Nolo's summary of the statutes. A tax foreclosure can also wipe out a mortgage because the tax lien has priority.

We buy Morton County houses as they are, including homes in Mandan and in the smaller towns, and we work with your title company on the county payoff.

More questions about Morton County, ND Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Morton County?

The Morton County Treasurer, at 210 2nd Ave NW in Mandan. The office phone is 701-667-3310.

Does Mandan assess its own property?

Yes. The City of Mandan runs its own assessing and building inspection departments for properties inside city limits, while the county assesses unincorporated areas and contracting towns.

When is Morton County property tax due?

Taxes are due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1. Paying in full by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount, and the second installment date is October 15.

What date does Morton County foreclose tax liens?

The tax lien foreclosure date is October 1 at 5 p.m. The county's annual sale of delinquent property falls on the third Tuesday of November.

Which credits can reduce a Morton County property tax bill?

The Homestead Credit, the Disabled Veterans Credit and the Primary Residence Credit. The homestead income limit listed by the county is $70,000 after medical deductions.

Who to contact in Ward County

  • Ward County Treasurer

Selling in Ward County?
We buy Ward County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Ward County by the numbers

Where is Ward County, North Dakota, and what is in it?

Ward County sits in north-central North Dakota, and its county seat and largest city is Minot. The county covers about 2,056 square miles, of which roughly 2,013 are land, according to the Census-based figures on its Wikipedia entry. It borders Renville County to the north, McHenry County to the east, McLean County to the south and Mountrail County to the west, with Burke County touching its northwest corner.

The legislature created the county on April 14, 1885 and it was organized that November 23. It carries the name of Mark Ward. The 2020 census counted 69,919 residents, which made it the fourth-most populous county in the state.

Beyond Minot, the incorporated cities are Berthold, Burlington, Carpio, Des Lacs, Donnybrook, Douglas, Kenmare, Makoti, Ryder, Sawyer and Surrey. Minot Air Force Base is a census-designated place of its own, and parts of the Des Lacs, Hiddenwood and Upper Souris National Wildlife Refuges fall inside the county line. Most of the land outside the towns is farmland.

U.S. Highways 2, 52 and 83 cross the county, along with North Dakota Highways 5, 23, 28 and 50.

What drives the Ward County economy, and why does it matter to a seller?

Minot Air Force Base is the largest single employer in Ward County. The Minot Area Chamber EDC reported in February 2026 that the base generated $956.7 million in economic impact in fiscal year 2025, with total on-base employment estimated at 6,957 jobs and more than 11,000 people living on or tied to the base when service members, family members and civilian employees are counted. Details are in the chamber's economic impact announcement.

The chamber's own description of the region also points to agriculture, with 15 commodities that rank near the top nationally, and to the energy activity of the Bakken region. The Wikipedia entry for the county notes that the area is largely devoted to agriculture.

That mix shapes how houses sell. Service members move on orders, so a seller tied to the base may need a closing date they can plan around.

How is a Ward County house taxed?

North Dakota taxes a house on a taxable value equal to 4.5 percent of its true and full value, multiplied by the combined mill levy of every local taxing district. The Office of State Tax Commissioner explains the method. A mill is one tenth of one percent, so you multiply taxable value by 0.001 and then by the total mills on your statement.

State materials define assessed value as 50 percent of market value, and a residential building is one that provides separate family living quarters for fewer than four family units. Apartment buildings with four or more units are classed as commercial.

The State Tax Commissioner works through a sample of a $275,000 home with a 250-mill levy: $12,375 of taxable value, about $12.38 per mill, and $3,095 of tax. Ward County levies will differ, and the county treasurer's statement shows the real mills. As a rough illustration only, the Census median owner-occupied value shown earlier on this page, $259,100, produces a taxable value of $11,659.50 and about $11.66 per mill before any credits.

North Dakota offers a primary residence credit, a homestead property tax credit with a renter's refund, and a disabled veteran's credit. Each has its own eligibility rules on the state tax site, and a seller who has been claiming one should note that a buyer will need to qualify on their own.

When are Ward County property taxes due, and what is the penalty for paying late?

Real estate taxes in Ward County become due on January 1 of the year after the tax year, and the first installment is delinquent after March 1. The dates come from North Dakota Century Code chapter 57-20, which the county treasurer follows.

DateWhat happens
January 1Taxes for the prior tax year become due.
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5 percent discount (paid or postmarked).
March 1First installment is delinquent after this date; a 3 percent penalty applies.
May 1Another 3 percent penalty is added to unpaid first-installment taxes.
July 1Another 3 percent penalty is added.
October 15Second installment is delinquent after this date, with a 6 percent penalty; unpaid first-installment taxes pick up a further 3 percent.

The 5 percent discount applies to general real estate taxes paid in full by February 15, and the treasurer applies it before any primary residence credit. It does not apply to personal property taxes or special assessment installments. If county commissioners declare an emergency from weather or another catastrophe, they may extend the discount period by 30 days.

The statute also says that failing to receive a statement does not release an owner from liability. Ward County's property tax page says the same discount rule applies to mobile homes, and the county's online payments page says statements are printed to reflect the discount when full payment arrives by February 15.

How do you appeal a Ward County assessment?

Begin with the Tax Equalization office, then go to the local board of equalization in April, then to the county board, and finally to the State Board of Equalization. The Ward County Tax Equalization office is at 225 Third St. SE, Suite 232 in Minot, 58701, and its number is 701-857-6430. County guidance says that if you do not get satisfaction from the assessor, you can take the appeal to the local board of equalization.

County pages say a township board meets the second Monday in April, and the City of Minot says its City Board of Equalization meets the second Tuesday of April on a schedule set by the county tax director. The City of Minot lists a contact at 701-857-4108 for the city board. Dates can shift, so confirm them each year.

The state-level rule matters if you want to go further. A State Board of Equalization staff report cites NDCC 57-13-04.3, which requires anyone appealing to the state board to have applied to both the local and county boards first. You can also contact the State Property Tax division at propertytax@nd.gov or 701-328-3127 to start a state appeal, where you will complete a questionnaire and submit evidence.

  • Gather recent comparable sales and any appraisal.
  • Photograph defects the assessor may not know about.
  • Bring your notice and parcel number to the April meeting.

What should Ward County sellers know about winter and flooding?

Minot's cold is severe enough to matter to a house inspection. The National Weather Service lists a record low of minus 49 degrees Fahrenheit for Minot in February, and minus 47 in January, in its North Dakota climate extremes table. Furnaces, pipes and roofs in older homes take real wear from that, and a buyer's inspector will look.

Flooding is the other part of local memory. A U.S. Geological Survey summary of the 2011 Souris River flood says more than 4,000 homes in Minot flooded and about 11,000 people were evacuated. A city program tied to a floodplain buyout process aimed to give residents whose homes were damaged or bought out access to affordable housing, according to an adaptation case study.

Fifteen years after the flood, local television reporting in June 2026 returned to the topic of costly flood insurance premiums and coming changes to FEMA maps. A seller whose house sits near the Souris River should expect questions about flood zone status and insurance cost, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is can simply price that uncertainty rather than asking you to resolve it before closing.

What happens to unpaid property tax if you sell a Ward County house?

Unpaid property tax stays attached to the property, so it is normally paid out of your sale proceeds at closing. The title company will order a tax search and ask the county treasurer for the amounts due, including any penalty that has built up since March 1 or October 15.

Because installments carry 3 percent penalties that stack on a schedule, an owner who sold in the summer after missing the March 1 date would face the first 3 percent penalty plus the May 1 and July 1 additions. Paying before the next date stops the next penalty, and asking the treasurer for a payoff figure for a specific day avoids surprises.

  • Ask the county treasurer or your title officer for a written payoff good through the closing date.
  • Check for special assessments, which are not eligible for the 5 percent discount.
  • Confirm whether any primary residence or homestead credit you used will end with the sale.

On a cash sale, the same steps apply, but there is no lender underwriting to hold up the payoff.

More questions about Ward County, ND Property Tax Guide

When is the Ward County property tax discount deadline?

February 15. Pay all of the year's real estate taxes in full on or before that date, or have the payment postmarked by then, and the county treasurer allows a 5 percent discount under NDCC 57-20-09. Ward County says its statements are printed to reflect the discount.

Where do I mail a Ward County property tax payment?

The listing we confirmed gives the address as Ward County Treasurer, PO Box 5005, Minot ND 58702. Online payment is available by credit card or e-check, so check the county's online payments page before you mail anything.

How do I appeal my Ward County assessment?

Talk to the Ward County Tax Equalization office first, then take your case to the township or city board of equalization in April, then the county board. A state appeal requires that you applied to the local and county boards first.

What is the penalty if I miss March 1?

A 3 percent penalty applies to the first installment of real estate tax after March 1. Further 3 percent penalties are added on May 1, July 1 and October 15, and the second installment carries a 6 percent penalty if it is not paid by October 15.

Can I sell a Ward County house that still has tax due?

Yes. The unpaid amount, with any penalty, is paid from the proceeds at closing. A buyer who purchases as-is for cash can close on a timeline that suits you, and the title company settles the tax with the treasurer.

Who to contact in Cass County

  • Cass County Finance Office

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Assessor values reviewed by city/township boards, county director of equalization, county board, then State Board
  • Penalties real estate: 3% after Mar 1, then +3% May 1, Jul 1, Oct 15 (12% total on 1st installment); 2nd installment 6% after Oct 15; prior years 1% per month; $50 fee with foreclosure notice at 3 years delinquent
  • Payment: online e-check and cards (convenience fee), in person at Finance Office, mail (postmark), drop box in front of Courthouse

What we could not confirm

  • Cass County mobile home penalties exist (see collector page) but not tabulated

Cass County by the numbers

What is Cass County, North Dakota?

Cass County is the most populous county in North Dakota, on the state's eastern edge along the Red River, and Fargo is its seat and largest city. The Dakota Territory legislature defined it on January 4, 1873, and it was organized on October 27 of that year. It is named for George Washington Cass, president of the Northern Pacific Railway from 1872 to 1875.

The county covers 1,767.8 square miles, almost all of it land. The Red River flows north along the eastern boundary with Minnesota. The terrain is low rolling hills, mostly farmed except around developed areas, sloping to the north and east, with the highest point at 1,194 feet in the southwest corner. The 2020 census counted 184,525 residents and the 2025 estimate is 201,794, about a quarter of the state's population.

The county is part of the Fargo-Moorhead metropolitan area. Interstates 29 and 94 cross it, along with US 10, 52 and 81, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops in Fargo. MATBUS runs local transit.

Which cities and school districts are in Cass County?

Cass County has 27 incorporated cities, and your city and school district decide which mill levy applies to your house. The list includes Fargo, West Fargo, Casselton, Kindred, Horace, Mapleton, Hunter, Tower City, Enderlin and smaller places such as Alice, Amenia, Ayr and Page.

School districts named for the county include Fargo Public Schools, West Fargo Public Schools, Kindred, Central Cass, Northern Cass, Maple Valley, Enderlin Area, Hope-Page, May-Port CG and Mapleton, which covers only the elementary grades. Some cities sit in more than one district, so one city can have several levies:

Taxing combinationTotal mills listed by the county
City of Fargo, Fargo School District298.43
City of Fargo, West Fargo School District289.98
City of Fargo, Kindred School District287.70
City of West Fargo306.19
City of Casselton282.41
City of Horace, West Fargo School District285.88
Barnes Township, Fargo School District206.74

These come from the examples in the county's property tax calculator, so check the year on your own statement. A Fargo house in the West Fargo school district, for instance, has a lower total than the same value in the Fargo district.

What should a seller know about Fargo?

Fargo had 125,990 residents in the 2020 census and covers about 50.8 square miles. It was founded in 1871 and incorporated in 1874. Fargo Public Schools serves most of the city, and West Fargo Public Schools serves the southwestern part.

Large employers include Sanford Health (6,278 full-time equivalent staff), Essentia Health (2,848), West Fargo Public Schools (2,541), North Dakota State University (2,167), Fargo Public Schools (2,064) and the VA Health Care System (1,380). Hector International Airport and the two interstates connect the city.

Cold is part of the house. Fargo's January mean is 9.2 degrees Fahrenheit, July is 70.7, and snowfall averages 51.4 inches a season, with a recorded low of minus 48 and a high of 114.

How does flood history affect a Cass County house sale?

The Red River crested at 39.5 feet in 1997 and 40.84 feet in 2009, and the Fargo area has responded since with sandbagging, infrastructure upgrades, buying houses in flood-prone areas and the FM Diversion project.

For a seller, that history turns into three practical questions:

  • Is the lot in a mapped flood zone, and does the buyer's lender require flood insurance?
  • Has the basement taken water, and is there a sump pump or backup system you should disclose?
  • Did the city or county buy out nearby lots, which could change the street?

Flood facts are not part of your tax bill, but they can affect how a buyer prices the house, so be ready to answer them truthfully.

Who assesses property in Cass County?

The Cass County Tax Equalization office, led by Director Matt Stanger, handles assessment, and the Finance Office bills and collects the tax. The assessor's office is in the Courthouse at 211 9th Street South, Fargo, ND 58103, phone (701) 241-5616. The Finance Office, in the same building, answers at (701) 241-5600.

Assessed value is 50 percent of true and full value, which is market value for residential and commercial property and productivity value for agricultural land. Taxable value is 9 percent of assessed value for residential property and 10 percent for other property. Net consolidated tax adds the taxing entities' mill levies, multiplies by taxable value and subtracts state-paid property tax relief, which the county ties to N.D.C.C. 57-20-07.1.

Cass County also provides a property info site at cass.northdakotaassessors.com and an interactive sales app that shows sales near a parcel. Its exemptions fall into two groups: discretionary ones, such as economic expansion, new home construction or remodeling, and non-discretionary ones, such as government, school, church and park property. It also lists a farm residence exemption, a homestead property tax credit and a disabled veteran credit.

What are the Cass County tax dates and penalties?

Statements are mailed in the first week of December. The first installment of real estate tax is due March 1 and the second October 15. A 5 percent discount comes off the consolidated tax if the full amount is paid by February 15, but it does not apply to specials and drain taxes. When a deadline falls on a weekend or county holiday, it moves to the next business day.

DateFirst installment and specialsSecond installment
March 13%n/a
May 16%n/a
July 19%n/a
October 1512%6%

Taxes from prior years accrue interest at 1 percent per month for real estate, added on the first of the month. You can pay online by e-check or card (card use adds a convenience fee), in person at the Finance Office, by mail, or in the secure drop box in front of the Courthouse. The statement carries a parcel number that does not change unless the parcel is split or combined, and a statement number that changes every year.

How do you appeal a Cass County assessment?

Cass County describes three steps, and the first is a phone call. Contact the Tax Equalization office at 701-241-5616 to handle concerns informally. Then you can appear before the boards of equalization.

  1. City Board of Equalization, held within the first 15 days of April
  2. County Board of Equalization, held within the first ten days of June
  3. State Board of Equalization, held the second Tuesday of August, which you can reach only if you appeared before both the city and county boards

If you missed the boards, you can file a formal abatement. The county says it must be filed no later than November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent, in duplicate, and physically mailed. The statute is N.D.C.C. 57-23-04, and the form is on the State Tax Commissioner's site.

What happens when Cass County property tax is delinquent?

The Finance Office mails a letter at each stage. Statements of Taxes Owing go to owners with delinquent real estate tax in March, May, July and October. A Notice of Tax Lien goes out in November and explains when interest begins and how foreclosure works. In May, certified mail brings a Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien to parcels delinquent for three years, and a $50 fee is added to those parcels.

Mobile homes follow a different path: a Warning and Notice for Delinquent Taxes in August for taxes delinquent one year, then a sheriff's letter about ten business days later, and eventually a sale at the front door of the Courthouse. The county notes that penalty details for mobile homes are on the collector page.

How does a Cass County house sale handle unpaid tax?

The title company pays unpaid property tax from your proceeds at closing. Ask the Finance Office for a payoff that runs through the closing date, because the March, May, July and October steps change the total. Special assessments and drain taxes are shown separately on the statement and also need to be cleared.

Renters make up a large share of Cass County, with about 48.8 percent of occupied homes rented in the 2020 census. That means many sellers are landlords, and a house sold with tenants should come with leases and rent records. We buy Cass County houses as-is, with or without tenants, and we do not quote a price before seeing the property. You owe nothing if you turn our offer down.

More questions about Cass County, ND Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay property tax in Cass County, ND?

Pay the Cass County Finance Office at the Courthouse, 211 9th Street South, Fargo. You can also pay online, by mail or in the drop box in front of the Courthouse.

How much is the late penalty in Cass County?

On the first installment and specials, 3 percent after March 1, then 6 percent on May 1, 9 percent on July 1 and 12 percent on October 15. The second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

Is there a discount for early payment in Cass County?

Yes. Paying the full consolidated tax by February 15 earns 5 percent off. It does not apply to special assessments or drain taxes.

When do the Cass County boards of equalization meet?

The city board meets in the first 15 days of April, the county board in the first ten days of June, and the State Board on the second Tuesday of August.

Can I sell a Cass County house with delinquent taxes?

Yes. The unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Request a payoff figure from the Finance Office at (701) 241-5600.

Grand Forks County by the numbers

What is Grand Forks County, North Dakota?

Grand Forks County is in eastern North Dakota, with the Red River forming its eastern border, and its county seat and largest city is Grand Forks. The Dakota Territory legislature created it on January 4, 1873, and county government was organized on March 2, 1875. Boundaries have been unchanged since 1883.

The county covers 1,439 square miles, mostly agricultural land outside the urban area, and slopes gently north and east. It had 73,170 residents in the 2020 census and an estimate of 74,501 for 2025, which makes it the third most populous county in the state.

Neighbors in North Dakota are Walsh, Traill, Steele and Nelson counties. Across the river are Marshall and Polk counties in Minnesota.

What places and landscapes make up the county?

Beyond the city of Grand Forks, the county includes small towns and farm townships, with Larimore and Northwood among the communities named in the school and township listings and Thompson also served by a school district. East Grand Forks, Minnesota, is a core city of the metro area but sits in another state and county.

School districts named for the county include Grand Forks, Thompson, Larimore and Northwood, so the district on your tax bill depends on where the parcel sits. The University of North Dakota, founded in 1883, is the state's oldest university and the only home of its medical and law schools, and it anchors the east side of the county.

The Forest River crosses the upper western part of the county. Turtle River State Park, Kellys Slough and Little Goose National Wildlife Refuges, and the Prairie Chicken State Game Management Area are listed among its protected lands. Fordville Dam, Larimore Dam and Smith Lakes are the reservoirs.

  • Urban property: values set by the City of Grand Forks Assessing Department
  • Rural and small town property: assessed with township and city assessors through the county
  • Mobile homes: handled through the county Tax Equalization Office

What does the economy look like for county property owners?

The county's economy blends farming with the education, health and defense jobs concentrated in the city. The University of North Dakota, Altru Health System and the Grand Forks Air Force Base are the three largest employers listed for Grand Forks, with Grand Forks Public Schools next.

Rural owners face a different tax picture than city owners because agricultural land follows its own valuation approach under state rules. Morton County's assessment page makes the same point, saying agricultural land is valued with a state agricultural valuation guide while homes are assessed at market value. Ask the county Tax Equalization Office which category your parcel falls into.

Which offices handle property tax in Grand Forks County?

The Tax Equalization Office values property with township and city assessors, the Treasurer bills and collects, and the Recorder keeps ownership records. The Tax Equalization Office and the Recorder are both at 151 South 4th Street, Grand Forks, ND 58201.

OfficeRoleContact
Tax Equalization OfficeUniform assessment, mobile home permits and statements701-780-8259 (director); mail to PO Box 5294, Grand Forks ND 58206-5294
County TreasurerBills and collects real estate tax701-780-8292; PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638
RecorderRecords documents affecting title701-780-8262; PO Box 5066

The county staff directory lists a Director of Tax Equalization, a Deputy Director, a Real Estate Assessor at 701-780-8245 and a Real Estate Tax Assistant at 701-780-8251. Staff change, so confirm the right extension when you call.

How do Grand Forks County property tax dates work?

Taxes are due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1, with a 5 percent discount for paying the full year by February 15. State law sets statements to be mailed by December 26.

StepDate
Valuation dateFebruary 1
City or township board of equalizationFirst 15 days of April
County board of equalizationFirst 10 days of June
State board of equalizationSecond Tuesday of August
Budget notices from the treasurerAugust 31
Statements postmarkedBy December 26
5% discount deadlineFebruary 15
Abatement applicationNovember 1 of the next year

If you split the year, the first installment is due March 1 and the second October 15. Under North Dakota Century Code section 57-20-01, a 3 percent penalty applies after March 1 and again on May 1, July 1 and October 15, and the second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

How can I look up a Grand Forks County parcel?

The county posts online search tools that cover both the county and the city. They include Vanguard house information searches for each, a Tyler iTax site for real estate and mobile home tax information, an ArcGIS parcel map, and iDoc for recorded documents.

  • Use iTax to see the current tax balance by address, owner name or property number
  • Use the Vanguard pages to see valuation details
  • Use iDoc to search recorded documents by grantor and grantee

The county's GIS page warns that the maps are for reference only and are not a legal description. Order a survey or title search if a boundary matters to your sale.

How do I challenge a Grand Forks County assessment?

Contact the assessor for your parcel first, then appeal to the local board in April and the county board in June. State law lets the State Board of Equalization reduce a value only if you appealed at both the local and county levels.

Each owner receives a written notice showing true and full value for the current and previous year. After the August state meeting, you can apply for abatement of the current year's assessment by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes payable. Forms are on the State Tax Commissioner's website.

A city property owner appeals through the city board, and written, phone or electronic appeals count as appearing in person.

What happens when Grand Forks County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid tax becomes a lien, and a parcel with taxes delinquent into the third year can be foreclosed by the county. The owner can stop that by paying all taxes, specials, interest, penalties and costs by October 1, following notice served by June 1.

The county posts a Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien on its website, and the 2026 notice is listed there. Once a county takes a tax deed, the former owner may buy back before resale, subject to the board of county commissioners.

A tax foreclosure can wipe out a mortgage, since the tax lien has priority. That is why servicers often advance the tax on loans without escrow and add it to the balance.

How does selling in Grand Forks County work when tax is due?

The unpaid amount is normally paid from your sale proceeds at closing, and the Recorder then records the deed. North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, so you pay recording fees only. The Recorder lists a $1.00 per page copy fee and $5.00 for the first page of a certified copy.

If you inherited a house or fell behind, ask the Treasurer for the full payoff and ask the city or township about specials. A cash sale can close without a buyer's lender and appraisal, which removes one source of delay when a tax foreclosure date is near.

We buy Grand Forks County houses in any condition and handle the title company coordination, so the county balance is paid at closing.

More questions about Grand Forks County, ND Property Tax Guide

Where is the Grand Forks County Treasurer?

The Treasurer's mailing address is PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638, and the phone is 701-780-8292.

Who assesses property in Grand Forks County?

The Tax Equalization Office works with township and city assessors. The City of Grand Forks Assessing Department values property inside the city.

When is the discount deadline for Grand Forks County property tax?

February 15. Paying the full year by then earns a 5 percent discount, and the first installment is due March 1.

How many people live in Grand Forks County?

The 2020 census counted 73,170 people, and the 2025 estimate is 74,501.

Can I buy back a property after a county tax foreclosure?

Possibly. State law allows the former owner to repurchase before the county resells it, either in full or under an installment contract with the county commissioners.
